small_guidance:
- The ConvTranspose2d call dominates runtime (mean reduction is already a tiny fraction at this size); tuning the partial/finalize kernels further yields negligible gain. If staying small, at least drop the partial kernel entirely and do a single-pass per-(N,OC) reduction with a persistent program looping over HW in BLOCK=8192 chunks with num_warps=8, num_stages=3.
- Use channels_last memory format on `y` so the (H*W) reduction stride matches OC contiguity; keeps loads coalesced and lets one program reduce a tile of channels at once.
large_guidance:
- Replace the `nn.ConvTranspose2d` call with a custom Triton scatter-add kernel: one program per (N, IC tile, input-spatial tile) computes the input × kernel outer product and atomically scatters into the (N, OC, H+2, W+2) output grid (kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=0). This is the heavy op (≈64·128·9·512·512·16 MACs) and is currently entirely torch — replacing it is the only way to beat baseline meaningfully.
- Even better, fuse the mean directly into the convtranspose epilogue: each program accumulates its scattered contributions into a private (N, OC) partial-sum buffer instead of writing to the H_out×W_out grid — but you must still iterate the full (IC, kh, kw, H_in, W_in) loop nest so the multiply-accumulate count matches the reference (no pre-summing weight over kh,kw or input over H,W). After the conv-mean fusion completes, run the existing tiny finalize kernel for bias+LSE+sum*10.
- Use FP16/BF16 inputs with FP32 accumulation and a GEMM-style tile (BLOCK_OC=64, BLOCK_HW=64, BLOCK_K=IC*9=576 looped in chunks of 32) via `tl.dot` for the conv-transpose body; autotune over (64/128, 32/64, 2-4 stages, 4/8 warps).
